# Pull-request approval policy

## Summary

Two approval publishers are configured during a staged rollout. The legacy [`weighted-approval` workflow](../workflows/weighted-approval.yml) publishes the required `weighted approval` commit status and its `weighted approval decision` check run at their existing paths. The active ruleset `20925054` requires one approving review and that status. The pilot [`weighted-approval-machine` workflow](../workflows/weighted-approval-machine.yml) publishes the same decision as a status comment and an approving review from the machine account `deepseek-ai-harness`, and publishes only when the `DSH_APPROVAL_REVIEW_SCOPE` repository variable selects it. The machine workflow reads its credential from the `weighted-approval` deployment environment. The machine review counts toward the one-approval requirement, but the required status still blocks a pull request below the weighted threshold; ruleset `27532727` stays disabled. Reviewers are chosen manually; an eligible delegation command requests review from its recipient.

<a id="approval-scoring"></a>

## Approval scoring

Both publishers evaluate an approval score from the repository default branch. The policy holds when counted approvals reach two points, the pull request is ready for review, and no write-capable reviewer has an effective `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review. Both publishers re-evaluate on open, reopen, head updates, base-branch changes, and transitions to or from draft. A title or description edit alone does not re-evaluate the score. Review submissions and dismissals, but not review-body edits, trigger the no-permission [`weighted-approval-review-event` workflow](../workflows/weighted-approval-review-event.yml); its validated run title and current head identify the pull request for both publishers. Conversation comment events run a publisher only when the current or previous body contains `/delegate`. Closed or merged pull requests and superseded heads are skipped before API writes. Each publisher serializes scoring runs per pull request. Prose-only edits and ordinary conversation comments do not replace a queued scoring run.

Reviewers whose calculated base repository permission is `write` or `admin` count. The [approval policy](approval-policy.json) gives `@07akioni`, `@CreatixChu`, `@imccyu`, `@LegGasai`, `@tianyicui`, `@tianyicui-bot`, `@turtle1999`, and `@turtle2099` two points each; every other write-capable reviewer gets one point. The pull-request author’s own review and reviewers without write permission do not count. Both publishers identify the machine account’s review by numeric user ID and exclude it from scoring, so that review cannot complete the threshold it is evaluating.

The PR author contributes `min(100, mergedPRCount) × 11 / 1000` points: 0 merged PRs → 0 points, 50 → 0.55, and 100 or more → 1.1. The publisher counts only merged PRs in this repository using the author’s immutable account ID, excluding the current PR. It stops at 100 matches and rejects incomplete history responses. Counts refresh at the next subscribed evaluation event. Author credit is separate from reviewer approvals and cannot satisfy the two-point requirement alone; the author’s own review remains excluded. Human and bot authors, including Dependabot, use the same rule, except that PRs authored by `@turtle2099` receive a fixed 0.2 points without a history lookup. Drafts, blocking reviews, and sufficient reviewer points skip history lookup; logs mark credit as not evaluated. Otherwise, logs show author credit and the capped count, or the fixed credit, separately. Below the cap, counting may scan the repository’s entire merged history; a failed required lookup fails the evaluation.

A one-point approval receives weight `min(2, 1 + 4 × ownedLines / totalLines)` from modified or deleted old production-code lines, attributed by `git blame` at the merge base of the live base branch and exact reviewed head. Ownership of 0%, 12.5%, and 25% gives 1, 1.5, and 2 points; higher ownership remains capped at 2. The success threshold remains 2 total points, without rounding the score. New lines do not enter the denominator, and an empty denominator gives no boost. Existing two-point weights remain unchanged. GitHub commit-author accounts identify reviewers across author emails; unlinked authors remain in the denominator without contributing to a reviewer. The publisher logs measured ownership. It skips attribution when reviewer points plus author credit already meet the threshold or a blocking review exists. Displayed scores use at most three decimal places; the decision uses unrounded scores with a tolerance of `1e-12` points for floating-point error. The curve endpoints come from the policy’s default and required points.

Production source means supported code files under `src/` in `packages/`, `apps/`, `python/`, and `native/`, plus the Desktop renderer, Python interpreter scripts, and committed runtime/packer launchers. The [classifier](blame-production.py) excludes documentation, tests, fixtures, snapshots, test support (including `src/testing/` and `src/testing.ts`), examples, generated source, dependencies, vendored code, declarations, comments, and blank lines. Pygments lexers distinguish comments from strings; mixed code/comment lines count, as do C preprocessor directives. Classification uses the old path and content, so changes to the PR’s file locations or generated headers cannot remove old lines from the denominator. Pure renames have no changed lines; renames with edits use the old path for blame.

Each reviewer contributes only the current `APPROVED` or `CHANGES_REQUESTED` decision that GitHub returns. A `DISMISSED` record clears that reviewer's standing decision, including earlier approvals. Comment-only and pending records do not replace a decision. Reviews from deleted accounts and reviewers without current repository access do not count. The workflows do not invalidate an approval by its review commit; the repository's native pull-request rules own stale-review and latest-push requirements.

Each publisher fetches every review and conversation comment, then resolves current repository permission before deciding. Permission changes take effect on the next subscribed event.

<a id="legacy-status-publisher"></a>

## Legacy status publisher

The legacy workflow writes the `weighted approval` commit status on the pull-request head. It writes `pending` below two points, while the pull request is a draft, or while a write-capable reviewer has an effective `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review; it writes `success` only when the threshold is met and no such blocker exists; it writes `error` when setup or evaluation fails. The publisher marks the head pending before Python setup or lexer installation, so failed setup or an interrupted history fetch cannot leave a previous success in place. Ruleset `20925054` requires that status. Keep GitHub Actions as its expected source; a context-only requirement can accept a same-named status from another integration.

The legacy workflow also writes the `weighted approval decision` check run, which reports the same decision as a conclusion: `action_required` while the policy is unmet, `success` when it holds, and `failure` on setup or evaluation failures, with the score or blocker in its title. The check run is not required by branch rules. It is published with a token minted from the approval App (`checks: write`), because GitHub attaches a check run created with the job token to the earliest Actions check suite on the head, and the merge box omits that run when the suite belongs to this `pull_request_target` workflow. The status uses the job token; a failed App token step or check-run write is logged and never changes the status. The [decision about the commit status](../../.agents/notes/archived/process/2026-10-20-weighted-approval-status-gate-with-check-run-label.md) records the measured check-run association and the job-token fallback.

<a id="pilot-review-publisher"></a>

## Pilot review publisher

The pilot writes no commit status and no check run. When its policy is unmet, the machine account `deepseek-ai-harness` writes one conversation comment containing `<!-- weighted-approval -->`. The comment carries the current score, counted approvals with their ownership or delegation, remaining points, blocking change requests, delegated reviews still awaited, and reviews without write access. Each evaluation updates that comment in place, and the publisher deletes it when the policy holds or the pull request becomes a draft. A comment marker copied by another account is ignored because the publisher identifies its own comments by the machine account’s numeric user ID, `359032549`.

When the policy holds, the pilot submits an `APPROVE` review carrying the same marker, the final score, and the evaluated commit ID, and deletes the status comment only after the review is recorded; a failed submission leaves the comment in place. It submits no review when its latest review is already `APPROVED` for that commit. When the policy stops holding, the pilot dismisses every marked machine-account `APPROVED` review, then posts or updates the comment. A draft dismisses those reviews and removes the comment instead. The dismissal message is `Weighted approval no longer holds.`.

Before submitting an approval, the pilot re-reads the pull request and fails the run when it is no longer open or ready, or its head changed. The review names the evaluated commit ID, and the pilot verifies that the returned review names the same commit.

The pilot does not dismiss its approval before evaluating, because dismissing it would itself be a review event and start another evaluation. After identity verification, a scoring failure attempts to dismiss every marked machine-account approval and then fails the run. Setup, credential, or API failures and undelivered events can still leave an earlier approval, so the pilot is not fail-safe on those paths; the team requirement is not enabled until they are verified. Drafts are never approved; the pilot retracts a previous marked approval and removes the status comment.

Stale-review dismissal is off in both the active ruleset `20925054` and the disabled ruleset `27532727`; last-push approval is off in both. A push after publication does not retract the approval automatically; the next evaluation re-scores the new head and retracts or republishes the approval. An explicit dismissal of the machine approval while the policy still holds starts another evaluation, which submits a new approval for the current head. Workflow runs are asynchronous, so a pull request can briefly show an approval for an earlier commit. Check the reviewed commit before treating the approval as covering the current head.

<a id="rollout"></a>

## Rollout

The `DSH_APPROVAL_REVIEW_SCOPE` repository variable controls the pilot publisher:

- Unset: the pilot publisher is disabled and writes nothing.
- An exact decimal pull-request number: only that pull request is published, for the pilot.
- `all`: open pull-request events are published broadly.

A maintainer can re-evaluate one open pull request with the `workflow_dispatch` input `pull_number`. A dispatch is accepted only from the default branch and only when the scope is `all` or that pull-request number.

Before the pilot covers a second pull request, verify on one isolated pull request that the `evaluate` job reaches the `weighted-approval` environment and reads the token on all three trigger paths: the `pull_request_target` run, the `workflow_run` from the review-event workflow, and the delegated `workflow_call` from the legacy publisher after a confirmed dismissal. The merged #9005 probe measured only manual `workflow_dispatch` runs against a dedicated probe environment: the protected job read the marker at `master`, the same job was rejected before any step at a topic branch, and a separate control job without the environment ran at the topic branch and asserted the marker absent. It does not cover those three paths. Confirm each run records a deployment for that environment and the publisher completes its identity check and write. Set the scope to that pull request's number for the test and do not set `all` until all three pass. The pilot remains disabled while the variable is unset.

The variable does not change how the legacy publisher calculates or publishes the required status. When that publisher confirms a delegated human review was dismissed, it calls the machine workflow for the selected PR. A dismissal made with `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not itself start a review workflow. The called and standalone machine jobs share one concurrency group per PR and read the current review state before writing.

Ruleset `27532727` stays disabled while the pilot runs and adds no separate requirement. The active ruleset `20925054` requires one approving review and the `weighted approval` status: the machine review counts toward the one-approval requirement, but a pull request below the weighted threshold stays blocked by the status. No additional enforcement is added before the pilot’s error behavior, latency, and stale-approval behavior are verified. The legacy status requirement is not retired before the required review team below is verified.

<a id="required-review-team"></a>

## Required review team

After the pilot verifies comment updates, approval submission, dismissal, head binding, error behavior, latency, and stale-approval behavior, re-evaluate every open pull request the requirement will cover and inspect its published comment or approval. Then prepare ruleset `27532727` with one required reviewer: a team whose only member is `deepseek-ai-harness`, covering all files. Add one `required_reviewers` entry with `minimum_approvals: 1` and `reviewer` of type `Team`, configure its file patterns to match the files the requirement covers, and enable the ruleset only after the disposable-branch test below passes.

On a disposable target branch, confirm that GitHub accepts the singleton team as a required reviewer with repository access. Create an isolated ruleset whose include condition names only that exact branch, add the team there, and delete the ruleset after the test; do not add the team to rulesets `20925054` or `27532727` for the test and do not apply the test ruleset to production branches. Use PRs changing root files, dotfiles, and nested files. An unrelated user's approval must leave the team requirement unsatisfied; a valid approval from the machine account must satisfy it. Also inspect the PR Checks view and commit status: a publisher that does not call the Checks API can still have GitHub Actions job entries. Do not remove the old requirement based only on a rule's JSON or a workflow run's conclusion.

No enforcement is added before those checks pass. Do not add the team or retire the legacy status before that verification: a pilot failure would then block every pull request. The machine account cannot approve a pull request it authored, and a human approval cannot satisfy the singleton-team requirement, so do not open machine-authored pull requests on covered refs. After verifying the team requirement, remove the legacy required status before stopping its publisher. Preserve delegation reconciliation in the replacement before stopping the legacy job.

<a id="delegating-points"></a>

## Delegating points

Post `/delegate @username` as the entire text of a PR conversation comment to transfer your reviewer points to that user's effective `APPROVED` decision on this PR. For example, `/delegate @turtle1999` lets @turtle1999's approval count your points alongside their own. Until they approve, your points do not count, even if your own approval remains active. The legacy publisher reconciles every active eligible command: it dismisses the sender's existing `APPROVED` and `CHANGES_REQUESTED` reviews, then requests review from recipients who have neither approved nor already been requested. The pilot reads the same commands for scoring but does not dismiss human reviews or request reviews. This also handles commands posted on drafts once the PR becomes ready and commands whose original event was replaced in the concurrency queue. Other requested reviewers remain unchanged. The command does not submit a review; drafts do not dismiss or request reviews. Comment-only and pending reviews cannot be dismissed. A failed dismissal fails the legacy evaluation and prevents review requests; scores are refreshed after successful dismissal. Request failures are logged without changing the decision, and subsequent legacy evaluations retry outstanding requests.

Both accounts must currently have write or admin permission, and neither may be the PR author. Commands involving ineligible accounts are ignored. A sender's newest surviving eligible, author-authorized command wins, in comment creation order; editing an older comment does not move it after newer comments. Submitting any review after delegation automatically takes the points back, including an approval, change request, or comment-only review. Submitting an inline diff comment with “Add single comment” also creates a comment-only review and reclaims the points. Pending reviews do not count; a later dismissal does not restore the delegation. When timestamps are equal, the review takes precedence. A new command after the review can delegate again; editing an older command cannot reactivate it. Post `/delegate @your-own-username` to restore your own review decision. Editing or deleting a command recomputes delegation from remaining comments, so deleting the latest command can restore an older one. Quoted commands, code blocks, review bodies, inline review comments, and commands mixed with other text do not count. Surrounding whitespace is allowed; account matching is case-insensitive. An edited command is accepted only when GitHub identifies the original author as its latest editor; edits by other accounts cannot delegate or cancel that author’s points.

Each sender contributes at most once, using their own fixed weight or production-line ownership. A delegate can receive points from multiple senders, but can transfer only their own points: delegated points are not forwarded through another delegation. Author credit cannot be delegated. Other reviewers' effective `CHANGES_REQUESTED` decisions still block the PR. The sender's old reviews are dismissed through GitHub, so their old change request stops blocking only after dismissal succeeds. That dismissal retains the original submission timestamp and does not cancel delegation; only a review submitted by the sender at or after the command automatically reclaims their points. Dismissing or replacing the delegate's approval removes the counted points but leaves the delegation active for the delegate's next approval. Logs identify each counted score owner and their delegate. Comment history failures or the 3,000-record limit fail evaluation instead of accepting a partial history.

<a id="security"></a>

## Security

All actions in both jobs are pinned to commit SHAs. Each job checks out only the repository default branch. Neither job checks out or executes pull-request code. Pull-request reviews and comments are treated as API data and escaped in logs. Both publishers verify command authors and latest editors by immutable account ID through GraphQL, matching the body to the REST comment history before counting points or acting. Missing or inconsistent editor metadata fails evaluation. Non-author edits are ignored. The legacy publisher reconciles only active eligible delegations; superseded or revoked commands have no effects.

The legacy status job’s only secret is the approval App private key, used to mint a `checks: write` token for the decision check run; the status and history fetch use the job token. Fetch credentials exist only in the Git child environment. Missing history, parsing failures, or incomplete author queries fail evaluation rather than producing a partial score.

The pilot writes only with `secrets.DSH_APPROVAL_BOT_TOKEN`, the PAT of `deepseek-ai-harness` (user ID 359032549). The `evaluate` job declares `environment: weighted-approval` as a literal; that fixed environment supplies the value. The reusable workflow's `workflow_call` declares `DSH_APPROVAL_BOT_TOKEN` with `required: true`, and the legacy publisher that calls it forwards only the name (`DSH_APPROVAL_BOT_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DSH_APPROVAL_BOT_TOKEN }}`), not `inherit`. The caller must pass the name even though the called job's environment supplies the value; an environment secret takes precedence over a same-named repository or organization secret. The standalone triggers are unchanged: their `evaluate` job declares the same environment and reads the secret directly. The environment admits deployments only from `master`, has no tag rule, and disables administrator bypass. Store the PAT only as an environment secret, remove any repository secret with the same name, and remove this repository's access to a same-named organization secret; a job without the environment could read either copy. `required: true` fails a caller that omits the secret but does not prove the environment secret has a value; the pilot's token identity check rejects a missing or wrong value before any write. [Passing inputs and secrets to a reusable workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/reuse-automations/reuse-workflows) documents the name-only pass and the environment precedence. Before any write it verifies that the token belongs to that account by numeric ID and login. It mints no App token and holds no App private key. `productionOwnership` fetches Git history with the read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so the PAT is not used for that fetch. The publisher recognizes its own comments and reviews by the numeric account ID, so a marker copied by another account is ignored even when the text matches. Only when there is no blocker, reviewer points plus author credit are insufficient, and an approval has the policy’s default weight, the pilot fetches complete history, passes Git objects to the trusted classifier as data, and resolves commit authors in batches of 50. The review-event workflow has no `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions and passes only a decimal pull-request number in its run title. The pilot accepts only successful `pull_request_review` runs from the review-event workflow file, identified by `workflow_run.path`; GitHub can populate `workflow_run.name` with the expanded run title. The pilot rejects an invalid run title and a number that does not resolve to the workflow run's current pull-request head. During coexistence, the legacy publisher remains the sole writer for delegated human-review dismissals and review requests; the pilot writes only its own comment, its own approving review, and the dismissal of its own approval. Dismissal failures fail the evaluation; request failures remain separate from the approval decision.

Approval policy changes take effect only after they merge into the default branch. This prevents an untrusted pull request from changing the program or policy for its own run.

<a id="verification"></a>

## Verification

Run `pnpm run test:approval-policy` for policy parsing, effective review decisions, review-event validation, merged-history pagination and account matching, lazy author credit, permission filtering, weighted scoring, delegation conservation and revocation, editor authorization, comment pagination, dismissal and review-request reconciliation, blockers, drafts, closed-PR skips, legacy status publication, pilot comment and approving-review publication, retraction, scope selection, identity matching by account ID, and API failures. [Workflow tests](../../scripts/ci-workflow.spec.ts) pin the trusted checkout, the no-permission review handoff, the legacy status and App label tokens, the literal `weighted-approval` environment on the evaluate job, the required `workflow_call` secret declaration and the caller forwarding only its name, the pilot PAT, the absence of App token minting in the pilot, the scope variable, the workflow-dispatch input, events, and commands. The repository gate graph runs the approval policy and workflow tests in CI. The Python SDK job runs `uv run --python 3.10 --with-requirements .github/review-ownership/requirements.txt python -m unittest discover -s .github/review-ownership -p 'test_*.py'` for real Git histories, lexers, renames, shallow-history rejection, and the publisher’s fetch/analysis integration.
